- The delta between point estimates is 0.72 (0.58 minus -0.14, arithmetic from [c3]), but the scales may not be commensurate, so this is not a meaningful ratio.
- The 2018 interval excludes zero. The 2013 interval includes zero.

## Evidence
- [r1] 2018, Journal of Postgraduate Medicine, review tier (rank 4), doi 10.4103/jpgm.jpgm_571_17. Supports. "Pooled mean effect size for vitamin D supplementation on depressive symptom ratings in major depression was 0.58 (95% confidence interval, 0.45–0.72)." [c1]
- [r2] 2008, Journal of Internal Medicine, article tier (rank 3), doi 10.1111/j.1365-2796.2008.02008.x. Supports. "In the two groups given vitamin D, but not in the placebo group, there was a significant improvement in BDI scores after 1 year." [c1]
- [r3] 2012, Acta Paediatrica, article tier, doi 10.1111/j.1651-2227.2012.02655.x. Case series without a control, so it failed source-fit and is not counted as support. "There was a significant amelioration of depression according to the MFQ-S (p < 0.05)." [c1]
- [r4] 2025, J Steroid Biochem Mol Biol, trial tier (rank 5), doi 10.1016/j.jsbmb.2025.106698. Compares 4000 vs 600 IU/day, not placebo, so it is a weak contradiction. "Vitamin D3 4000 IU/day in AAs with T2DM did not produce significant difference in mental and functional health scores compared to 600 IU/day." [c1]
- [r5] 2013, J Clin Endocrinol Metab, review tier, doi 10.1210/jc.2013-3450. Contradicts. "Results of the classical meta-analysis showed no significant effect of Vit D supplementation on postintervention depression scores (standardized mean difference = -0.14, 95% confidence interval = -0.41 to 0.13, P = .32...)." [c1]
- [r6] 2012, Am J Epidemiol, article tier, doi 10.1093/aje/kwr482. Contradicts, but it tests vitamin D plus calcium in older women. "The findings do not support a relation between supplementation with 400 IU/day of vitamin D(3) along with calcium and depression in older women." [c1]
- [r7] 2025, Biomolecules & Biomedicine, review tier, doi 10.17305/bb.2025.12331. Neutral. "However, it remains to be established through future research whether acute or chronic vitamin D supplementation could have a protective effect against the development of depression." [c1]
- Three 2025 meta-analyses were judged unrelated because they cover neuropathy, deficiency and suicide risk, or noncommunicable diseases generally [c1].

## Method and limits
- **Windows and gap to today (2026-10-23):** research 2017–2025 ends 2025-12-31 (about 10 months before today). News ends 2026-06-01 (about 5 months). the health literature index and readable papers end 2025. Patents end 2024 and arXiv 2005–2025 [c1].
- **Lane:** everything is lane "subject". The 16-paper intersection [c1] is the only part that touches the actual claim.
- **Coverage:** all tables passed reachability checks, which the tool says are not proof of ingest completeness [c1].
- **Censoring:** the newest period is excluded from each series because ingest lags publication [c3].
- **Match mode:** document selection was by subject in the title and outcome in the abstract [c1].
- **What counts are and are not:** counts are papers or articles on the topic, not trials of depression. Orientation labels reflect a paper's framing, not whether the claim is true. Claim counts are not papers [c1].
- **Cannot answer:** the effect in current RCT-based pooling, effects by dose or baseline vitamin D, long-term outcomes, and any quantitative read of news framing. Nothing was measured on read/unread beyond the 3 documents read [c1].
- **Interpretation:** the "low confidence" verdict and the advice to supplement only if deficient are my judgment. The deficiency advice is from background knowledge, not from these calls (est.).
